title: Vision Transformers and the Patch-Token Primitive

questions.question: A transformer expects a sequence, but an image is a grid. What is the ViT patch-token step?
options: Split the image into patches, flatten each, then project each patch to a vector.
Run a CNN feature extractor first, then feed only its final class score.
Flatten every pixel into a separate token and attend over the full image.
Turn each color channel into a separate text sequence of pixel values.
questions.explanation: ViT converts the 2D grid into a sequence by splitting it into fixed-size patches, flattening each patch’s pixel channels, and applying the same learned projection to each. A CNN class score or one-token-per-pixel sequence is a different representation and misses this patch-token design.

questions.question: Assume a 224x224 image, patch size 16, one CLS token, and no register tokens. What is the ViT input sequence length?
options: 14 tokens: one token for each patch row.
224 tokens: one token for each image row.
197 tokens: 14*14 patches plus one CLS token.
196 tokens: 14*14 patches with CLS excluded.
questions.explanation: Each side has 224/16=14 patches, so the grid contributes 14×14=196 tokens. The stated CLS token adds one, for 197 total; the 196 choice counts patches but omits CLS.

questions.question: For a 16x16 RGB patch, how many scalar pixel values enter the shared patch projection?
options: 768 values, from 16*16*3.
48 values, from 16*3 without patch height.
3 values, one average per color channel.
256 values, from 16*16 without color channels.
questions.explanation: A 16×16 patch has 256 pixel locations and three RGB values at each, so the projection receives 16×16×3=768 scalars. The 256 option counts spatial pixels but omits the color dimension.

questions.question: Why can 2D-RoPE support variable patch grids more naturally than a learned absolute-position table?
options: It maps each patch to a text token with an absolute word index.
It removes all positional information before attention is computed.
It rotates query and key vectors using each patch's row and column position.
It assigns a separate learned table entry to every possible image size.
questions.explanation: 2D-RoPE derives rotations from patch row and column, so it does not require one learned vector for each position in a fixed grid. An absolute table needs interpolation or resizing when the grid changes.

questions.question: A ViT develops high-norm artifact patches that hijack attention and hurt dense prediction. What addition does the lesson describe?
options: Add register tokens to absorb attention artifacts, then discard them at handoff.
Add more CLS tokens and retain them as the only visual content.
Add a larger learned position table and remove the patch projection.
Add one extra caption token for every high-norm patch.
questions.explanation: Register tokens act as attention sinks for high-norm artifact patches that otherwise hijack attention; they improve dense prediction and are discarded before patch tokens are handed to the LLM. Retaining only more CLS vectors would not preserve that patch-level content.

questions.question: A VLM needs visual detail from an image rather than one image-level class embedding. What should its vision tower pass to the LLM?
options: Only the CLS vector, dropping the patch-token outputs.
The register tokens, because they contain the image's full content.
The mean of all patch tokens, replacing their spatial details.
All patch-token outputs, skipping image-level pooling.
questions.explanation: When the LLM needs local visual detail, passing every patch token preserves spatially distinct evidence. Mean pooling or a CLS-only vector compresses the image to one representation, and registers are scaffolding rather than visual content.
